translation:
On the second day of the bright half of Magsar, Samvat 1737, Jivanji Maharaj was resting at the house of Bhagwandas and Dhanbai in Bhilapur. Then he had a dream: two young men, radiantly beautiful, came to fetch him, holding a red staff in hand. Namdevji, Kabirji, Dhana Bhagat, Seni, Pipa, Rohidas, and other devotees were waiting for him. Then Jivanji Maharaj made a promise that he would come after six months, once he had fulfilled the wishes (manorath) of his devotees, and for the sake of his devotees' wishes, he extended his own life. Great souls (maha purush) such as Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj come into this world for the welfare (kalyan) — through fellowship and holy company (samagam-sant sangat) — of souls like us. Moreover, they are all-powerful, capable souls (sarvashaktiman samarth atma), and so they come into this world of their own free will, and they return of their own free will from this world back to their own abode (dham). On the second day of the bright half of Magsar, Samvat 1737, he had lovingly made a promise of six months for the sake of his devotees. This promise of six months, made on the second of the bright half of Magsar, was completed on the second of the bright half of Jeth; but the festival of Janmashtami was near — two months and twenty-one days away — so he made a further promise, that he would come after celebrating the festival (ochhav) of Janmashtami. Then, knowing that he now had to depart, he began preparing to take leave of this world. He called his own dear ones (nij jan) and told them to prepare grain and other things to make the food offering (bhojan prasad). He also sent invitations to all the children and cowherds (bal-gopal) to be present.

There is a difference between devotees who worship God (Bhagwad bhakti) in general and the devotion of our uda-bhakts who are engaged in devotion to God. Other people besides us perform devotion in order to attain some one or another world — heaven (swarga), Vaikunth, Golok, Chandralok, Suryalok, Janalok, Tapalok, Aksharlok (dham), and so on. But Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has declared all these worlds, including Vaikunth, to be fleeting and impermanent (kshanbhangur). He has further shown that attaining them brings no benefit at all. For the Bhagavad Gita says, _kshine punye martya lokam vishanti_ (when merit is exhausted, those who have gone to that world must come back again to the world of mortals). Therefore he himself had no wish to go to any of these places; rather, he had decided to go to his own abode (Swadham). For all these places are called "loks" (worlds), and we have no right or claim over them — what belongs to the lesser gods cannot be called ours. If there is an Indralok, it belongs to Indra; but if someone like you or me were to go to that world on a visa, then when his visa expires he would again have to return to his original homeland. But whoever dwells permanently in his own homeland can be removed from it by nobody. Therefore Jivanji Maharaj went to Swadham, his own abode, and to nowhere else. Moreover, in his abode there is an assembly (mijlas) of great saints such as Sadguru Kabir; and that is why he asked those who came to fetch him, again and again, whether Kabirji was there. Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj is therefore not separate from Kabirji, but is a very limb of Sadguru Kabirji himself.

Jivanji Maharaj manifested on this earth by the command of Kabirji and other supreme beings, for the welfare of worthy souls. Twice Jivanji Maharaj pushed back death for the welfare of his devotees. In this way, when the promise made in the dream was fulfilled, the conversation he had with the messengers who came to fetch him was overheard by Panabai, the wife of his son Shyamdas.
